items.question: How should one progress through the stages of bliss toward the peaceful ground?
premises: One intent on complete rest should abandon the former stage and ascend to the higher stage.
The ground consisting of innate bliss follows the peaceful state.
Progression through stages is oriented toward that innate-bliss ground.
items.inference: Therefore the practitioner should sequentially transcend lower stages to reach the innate-bliss ground that leads to peace.
items.plain_english: Intent on complete rest, one should abandon the former stage and move to the higher one, because the ground of innate bliss follows upon the peaceful state.

items.question: What gives rise to the states of nirānanda and parānanda?
premises: Nirānanda and parānanda are connected with puruṣa and the unborn principle.
Bliss expands from the experience of undivided and divided masses of objects.
The character of these two states arises from that expansion of bliss.
items.inference: Therefore nirānanda and parānanda arise from the bliss generated by experiencing undivided and divided objects in relation to puruṣa and the unborn.
uncertainties: The exact referent of 'ajāta' (unborn) is context-dependent and may indicate a specific tattva.
items.plain_english: Nirānanda and parānanda, connected with puruṣa and the unborn, arise from the expansion of bliss produced by masses of undivided and divided objects of experience.

rows.grounds: describes the mode of the state

items.question: Where and how does the state of great bliss manifest?
premises: A wondrous state of great bliss follows a leftward course.
This state shines forth in the great abode of Bhairava.
That abode is consciousness which has assumed all.
items.inference: Therefore the state of great bliss manifests in the all-encompassing consciousness of Bhairava through a leftward mode.
uncertainties: The technical sense of 'vāmācārā' (leftward course) may carry ritual or energetic connotations.
items.plain_english: A wondrous state of great bliss, of leftward course, shines forth in the great abode of Bhairava, in consciousness that has taken all within itself.

items.question: How does great bliss continue within the all-encompassing triad?
premises: Great bliss becomes consciousness-bliss.
It proceeds again within a specific triad.
That triad has assumed all the right, left, and upper aspects.
items.inference: Therefore great bliss, transformed into consciousness-bliss, continues to unfold within the triad that integrates right, left, and upper.
items.plain_english: Great bliss, having become the bliss of consciousness, proceeds again in this triad that has taken in all the right, left, and upper aspects.

items.question: In what modes can phenomena appear within the triad that grasps duality and nonduality?
premises: The triad in every way grasps both duality and nonduality.
Phenomena may appear as undivided.
Phenomena may appear as divided or as both divided and undivided.
items.inference: Therefore within the triad that comprehends duality and nonduality, phenomena can manifest as undivided, divided, or both.
items.plain_english: In the triad whose nature is to grasp both duality and nonduality in every way, things may appear as undivided, or divided, or both divided and undivided.

items.question: How do beings arise in relation to the fivefold bliss and universal bliss?
premises: Beings are joined with the fivefold states of bliss beginning with innate bliss.
There is a state of intense universal bliss.
Beings arise from that state of intense universal bliss.
items.inference: Therefore beings, structured by the fivefold bliss states, arise from the state of intense universal bliss.
items.plain_english: Beings, joined with the five states of bliss beginning with innate bliss, arise from the state of intense, overflowing universal bliss.

items.question: What distinguishes the states of innate bliss and nirānanda?
premises: Innate bliss is founded only on resting in the subject aspect.
Nirānanda arises from resting only in emptiness.
Each state is defined by its specific locus of rest.
items.inference: Therefore innate bliss and nirānanda are distinguished by whether rest occurs in the subject aspect or in mere emptiness.
items.plain_english: Innate bliss is founded only on resting in the aspect of the subject, while the state of nirānanda arises from resting only in emptiness.

items.question: How does supreme bliss arise in relation to the field of objects?
premises: Supreme bliss arises from resting in the domain of the object.
The object field can be filled on all sides with the collision of infinite objects.
Resting in that fully filled object field gives rise to supreme bliss.
items.inference: Therefore supreme bliss fully arises when awareness rests in the object domain, even when it is filled with infinite objects.
items.plain_english: Supreme bliss also fully arises from resting in the domain of the object, when the object is filled on all sides with the collision of infinite knowables.

rows.grounds: compound describing the state or experiencer

items.question: What defines the state called great bliss?
premises: The means of knowing can be engaged in savoring.
All masses of knowers and knowns can be apprehended and devoured.
A state skilled in that devouring arises through such savoring.
items.inference: Therefore the state called great bliss is defined by savoring through the means of knowing and devouring the apprehension of all knowers and knowns.
items.plain_english: The state called great bliss arises from the means of knowing through the yoking of savoring; it is skilled in devouring the apprehension of all masses of knowers and knowns.

items.question: When does consciousness-bliss arise in its unconditioned fullness?
premises: One may attain a rest that is unconditioned and utterly full.
Consciousness-bliss is not nourished by the inert.
Such rest corresponds to that consciousness-bliss.
items.inference: Therefore when unconditioned and utterly full rest is attained, consciousness-bliss arises, independent of the inert.
items.plain_english: When one attains a rest that is unconditioned and utterly full, then indeed there is consciousness-bliss, which is not nourished by anything inert.

items.question: What characterizes the reality in which consciousness-bliss shines?
premises: In that reality there is no divided state having an inert form.
In that reality there is no division whatsoever.
That reality shines forth on all sides.
items.inference: Therefore the locus of consciousness-bliss is an undivided, non-inert reality that shines everywhere without limitation.
items.plain_english: Where there is no divided state of inert form, where there is no division at all, and which shines forth on every side.

rows.grounds: compound with possessive sense; sandhi dhāma+asmākam

items.question: What did the teacher identify as the abode of universal bliss?
premises: There is a reality of unstruck awareness nourished by supreme nectar.
The teacher declared that reality to be the abode of universal bliss.
This identification is presented as authoritative.
items.inference: Therefore the abode of universal bliss is unstruck awareness nourished by supreme nectar, as taught by the guru.
items.plain_english: Our teacher declared that very reality—unstruck awareness nourished by supreme nectar—to be the abode of universal bliss.

rows.grounds: relative clause with existential; sandhi yatra+asti
object to be established; sandhi for viśrāntiḥ

items.question: How should one establish rest where contemplative practices do not primarily apply?
premises: There are states where contemplation and similar practices have no primary applicability.
Rest must still be established in such states.
The yoga of heart-utterance provides the method for establishing that rest.
items.inference: Therefore where contemplative practices do not primarily apply, rest should be established through the yoga of heart-utterance.
items.plain_english: Where contemplation and other practices have no primary applicability, rest should be established there through the yoga of utterance in the heart.

rows.grounds: adverb qualifying rest; sandhi for samyak

items.question: What is the complete rest attained there called, and how is it brought about?
premises: Complete rest can be attained in that state.
That complete rest is called supreme nonduality.
It arises through the application of the breath-staff and the equalizing of before and after.
items.inference: Therefore the complete rest attained there is supreme nonduality, realized by equalizing before and after through the breath-staff practice.
uncertainties: The technical meaning of 'prāṇadaṇḍa' (breath-staff) is practice-specific.
items.plain_english: The complete rest attained there is called supreme nonduality; it comes about through the application of the breath-staff and the equalizing of before and after.

rows.grounds: long compound describing the yogic ground
ablative of comparison; sandhi for narāt

items.question: How is the yogin's ground distinguished from that of the ordinary person?
premises: The yogin abides on a ground described as sprinkled by the mansion of the pendant lotus tetrad.
Bondage and liberation are divided for the ordinary person.
The yogin's realization is situated elsewhere than that division.
items.inference: Therefore the yogin stands on a consecrated inner ground beyond the ordinary division of bondage and liberation.
uncertainties: The imagery of 'catuṣkikāmbujālambilambikāsaudha' is esoteric and may refer to a specific yogic diagram.
items.plain_english: By the yogin, elsewhere than in the ordinary person’s division of bondage and liberation, the ground is sprinkled by the mansion of the pendant lotus tetrad.

items.question: By what nature does the yogin operate in this realization?
premises: The yogin operates by an unsurpassed nature.
That nature functions through the activity of speech.
It is united with the dissolution and flourishing of the supreme I in reflective consciousness.
items.inference: Therefore the yogin acts from the unsurpassed nature that expresses itself through speech and the play of supreme I-consciousness.
items.plain_english: By the unsurpassed nature that operates through the activity of speech, united with the dissolution and flourishing of the supreme I in the reflective awareness of consciousness.

items.question: What illuminates and fills the field of experience in this yogic process?
premises: A sun whose nature is the true twelve phases is present.
That sun is emptied of the force of effort.
By it the entity is illuminated, filled, and fully pervaded.
items.inference: Therefore the effortless sun of the twelve phases illuminates, fills, and pervades the field of experience.
uncertainties: The 'twelve phases' likely refer to a specific esoteric solar or energetic schema.
items.plain_english: When the entity is illuminated by the sun—emptied of effort and whose nature is the true twelve phases—it is filled and fully pervaded.

items.question: What happens to the phases when the fire of awakening is entered?
premises: An agent possessing the sixteen named phases enters the fire of awakening.
The phases are slowed by the power of devouring that.
That agent completely releases the phases.
items.inference: Therefore entry into the fire of awakening by the sixteen-phased power leads to the complete release of the phases.
uncertainties: The identity of the 'sixteen named phases' is technical and context-dependent.
items.plain_english: Having entered the fire of awakening, the one possessing the sixteen named phases completely releases the phases, which are slowed by the power of devouring that.

items.question: What is attained by the one who has internalized all principles and reached emission?
premises: The agent has internalized infinite principles from ka to kṣa on all sides.
That agent has attained emission while remaining in an unchanged state.
Four life-giving powers are attained in that condition.
items.inference: Therefore the one who has internalized all principles and attained emission in an unchanged state obtains the four life-giving powers.
uncertainties: The 'four life-giving powers' are not named explicitly in this verse.
items.plain_english: By the one who has internalized the infinite principles from ka to kṣa on all sides, whose state remains unchanged after attaining emission, the four life-giving powers are attained.

items.question: What inner stance characterizes the yogin in relation to the beingness of all things?
premises: The yogin is joined to the heart where reflection on the essence of beingness is absent.
The yogin rests upon the eye of the yogin lineage fit for outward emission.
This stance concerns the beingness of all beings.
items.inference: Therefore the yogin abides in a non-reflective heart-essence while resting in the lineage-eye that governs outward emission.
uncertainties: The phrase 'yogikulanetra' is esoteric and may denote a specific lineage center or faculty.
items.plain_english: Joined to the heart where there is no reflection on the essence of the beingness of things, resting upon the eye of the yogin lineage fit for outward emission.

items.question: What stairway of powers is always established in the state of Rudra-union?
premises: A stairway-garland of powers is always established in the state of Rudra-union.
That stairway extends through consciousness, breath, quality, and body.
This structure is presented as permanently established.
items.inference: Therefore in the state of Rudra-union there is an ever-established stairway of powers spanning consciousness, breath, quality, and body.
items.plain_english: By the state of Rudra-union, that stairway-garland of powers—ending in consciousness, breath, quality, and body—is always indeed established.

items.question: How is the ground of emission approached through the power of vibration?
premises: Release occurs through emission moving within the womb of vibration.
After that release, the ground of emission is embraced.
That ground enjoys the state of the fish-womb.
items.inference: Therefore by vibratory emission one releases and embraces the emission-ground characterized by the fish-womb state.
uncertainties: The term 'matsyodaradaśā' is a technical yogic image whose precise referent is contextual.
items.plain_english: Then, having released through emission moving within the womb of vibration, one embraces the ground of emission, which enjoys the state of the fish-womb.

items.question: What supreme phase is reached upon ascending the ground of the trident?
premises: One ascends the ground of the trident connected with the three channels.
There is a supreme phase that is present in all, pervading all, and life-giving to all.
Ascending that ground gives access to that supreme phase.
items.inference: Therefore by ascending the trident-ground connected with the three channels, one reaches the supreme all-pervading, all-vivifying phase.
items.plain_english: Having ascended the ground of the trident, connected with the three channels, one reaches the supreme phase that is present in all, pervading all, and life-giving to all.

rows.grounds: object of resorting to; sandhi krameṇa+ekātmyam

items.question: What is the nature of the upper stairway of powers reached in this ascent?
premises: The ascent reaches a stairway-garland of powers ending in the brow-center, bindu, and nāda.
This stairway expands and contracts.
It resorts to unity in sequence.
items.inference: Therefore the upper stairway of powers, culminating in brow-center, bindu, and nāda, dynamically expands and contracts while maintaining sequential unity.
items.plain_english: One reaches the stairway-garland of powers ending in the brow-center, bindu, and nāda—expanding and contracting, and resorting in sequence to unity.
